newsitem.title: ISRAEL: EU tries to ease Mideast "danger" after U.S. fails.
newsitem.headline: EU tries to ease Mideast "danger" after U.S. fails.

text.p: The European Union, following hard on the heels of a failed U.S. attempt to revive moribund Israeli-Palestinian peace talks, pledged to redouble its efforts to resolve a crisis its Middle East envoy called "very dangerous".

But prospects of mediating a breakthough in the stricken peace process remained daunting, since Israel views the EU as siding firmly with the Palestinians and the Palestinians see the Clinton administration as tilting toward the Jewish state.

Hours after U.S. President Bill Clinton's lead Middle East troubleshooter Dennis Ross left after nine days of mediation attempts, the Palestinians said his mission's failure proved that Washington must reshape its policies if it was to rescue the talks.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi said the United States was in effect abandoning its long-held stance rejecting new Jewish settlement construction on occupied land.
Israeli-Palestinian talks halted two months ago after Israel began work on a new settlement in East Jerusalem.

Underscoring Palestinian restiveness over the deadlock, about 2,000 supporters of the militant Islamic Hamas movement massed in the West Bank town of Nablus on Saturday in a "Rally for Jerusalem" , denouncing the peace process in banners reading: "No compromise and no peace."
"The situation has become very dangerous," Miguel Angel Moratinos, the EU's Middle East envoy, said in Cairo. "The peace process must be saved."
Moratinos said he would go to Gaza on Sunday for talks with the Palestinians before holding meetings with Israel and co-sponsor Russia in a rekindled EU effort to seek a breakthrough.
"The European Union will do all it can through diplomatic channels to save the peace process," he said.
Israel has in the past resisted an EU role in negotiations, arguing that its views mirrored those of the Palestinians.

For its part, talks co-sponsor Washington, Israel's main ally, has toned down its rhetoric in an apparent nod to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hardline government, describing settlement as an issue to be resolved between the parties involved.

"The international community's position, including that of the U.S., on settlements is that they are illegal," Tibi said. "But the U.S. is now abandoning this position and adopting the Israeli position by hiding behind the pretext that settlements are a final-status issue."
Under the 1993 Israeli-Palestinian peace accord, settlements and Jerusalem are among volatile core issues left for "final status" talks to be completed by 1999.
The accord says no side should take unilateral actions that would prejudge the outcome of permanent status talks, stalled since Israel's right-wing government took office in June.

Palestinians say Israel violated the accord in March by starting to build a settlement in East Jerusalem, which Israel had declared part of its capital in a claim unrecognised internationally. The Palestinians see East Jerusalem as capital of a future Palestinian state.
Israel turned aside Palestinian criticism of U.S. policy and of its point man Ross. "Dennis Ross is a very fair mediator and is doing very a good job," Netanyahu aide Shai Bazak told Reuters.
Bazak also said the Palestine Liberation Oreganisation had as yet failed to satisfy Israel's demand for cooperation in the fight against guerrilla attacks.

Egypt laid the blame for the impasse squarely at Israel's door. Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said Israel's refusal to curb settlement on Arab land was responsible for the deadlock and he urged Washington to call its ally to order.

"The U.S. secretary of state (Madeleine Albright), due to her experience and position, enjoys a lot of influence which can benefit these difficult circumstances in which the doors of peace are being closed one after the other because of Israel's obstinacy," Moussa told reporters after talks with Moratinos.
Albright, who met Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on Friday, said she would visit the Middle East only when the parties made the "difficult decisions" required to break the deadlock.
